summary: Rastrojo is a decision-support tool that answers one question for a farm field: which crop rotation pays off, depending on who decides? In Argentina about 70% of farmland is rented, so the person who chooses the rotation is rarely the one who keeps the soil. Rastrojo compares rotations for four decision-makers (owner, tenant, cooperative and bank) against 41 real growing seasons (1984-2024) of NASA POWER weather, run through a daily FAO-56 water balance. Each rotation gets a score of margin plus soil change minus downside risk, with weights that depend on the decision-maker, and the tool says whether it is better to plant or to rent the field out. A search over 385 rotations marks the Pareto front. NASA GRACE-FO and SMAP L4 show today's water status. During the event we also prototyped two layers: a 25-year MODIS memory of what each field actually grew, and a climate twin that finds the place whose current climate and soil match the field under +1 to +3 C of warming. The engine is deterministic and auditable.
details:
THE PROBLEM
The same field is decided differently depending on who decides. In Argentina, 70.1% of the farmed area was worked under lease in the 2023/24 season (SISA data, Rosario Board of Trade). The owner thinks in decades and cares about the soil; the tenant thinks in one season and has tight working capital; the cooperative looks at volume; the bank looks at repayment risk. Same data, opposite decisions, and the soil pays the difference: only about 4 of every 10 kg of nutrients removed are replaced. Field Shift asks for a tool that helps farmers explore rotations that strengthen soil health and adapt to changing conditions. Rastrojo adds the question nobody models: for whom?

WHAT IT DOES
You pick who decides and Rastrojo answers, for that field: should I plant or rent it out, and which rotation? It compares the current rotation (continuous soybean) with four alternatives (maize/soybean, wheat/double-crop soybean then maize, maize/soybean with a rye cover crop, soybean with a vetch cover crop), shows each one month by month (crop, bare soil, frost), and explains why it ranks where it does, what evidence supports it, its risks and what data is missing. It also searches all 385 rotations of 1 to 3 seasons built from the crop catalog (277 pass the agronomic rules) and marks the Pareto front (84 rotations that no other beats at once on margin, soil and risk).

HOW IT WORKS
1. Climate: NASA POWER daily data at the field point, 1984-2024 (corrected precipitation, temperature, radiation, wind, humidity, root-zone wetness GWETROOT). 41 real seasons, classified as dry, normal or wet by rainfall terciles.
2. Water: a daily FAO-56 soil water balance with Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0) and crop coefficients (ETc = Kc x ET0). Initial moisture of each season comes from GWETROOT. Each rotation is feasible, risky or not feasible, season by season.
3. Soil: a soil index from -100 to +100 (cover, carbon, nitrogen, weeds, roots), months of bare soil and rain falling on bare soil.
4. Economics: gross margin per season by type of year.
5. Decision: J_u(r) = AF(i_u, H_u) x E(r) + alpha_u x dS(r) - lambda_u x AF(i_u, H_u) x ES_1/3(r), maximized over the feasible rotations. E(r) is the expected annual margin over the 41 seasons; AF(i, H) = (1 - (1+i)^-H) / i is the annuity factor that brings it to the horizon H and rate i of each decision-maker; dS(r) is the soil index; ES_1/3(r) is the expected shortfall of the worst third of the seasons. Owner: H 10 years, i 6%, alpha 5, lambda 0.3. Tenant: H 1, i 12%, alpha 0, lambda 0.5. Cooperative: H 5, i 8%, alpha 3, lambda 0.5. Bank: H 3, i 10%, alpha 0.5, lambda 1.5. These weights are example values to be validated with the local farmers' cooperative AFA.
6. Today's water: NASA GRACE-FO total water storage and SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture for the field, with their percentile.
The engine is 100% deterministic: same input, same output, no language model in the calculation. Every evaluation carries a SHA-256 hash, and every number carries its provenance (observed, derived, assumed or user input). Around 59 assumptions are listed with an id.

PROTOTYPES BUILT DURING THE EVENT (not yet integrated in the main app)
- Field memory: 25 seasons (2000-2024) of NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI (250 m, every 16 days) reconstruct what each pixel actually grew, using phenology rules. Over 16,659 pixels around the demo field, double cropping fell from 20-35% of the area to 1.2% in the 2008/09 drought and 4.4% in 2022/23. With April root-zone wetness from NASA POWER (the same variable the engine uses), the observed double-crop share was 14.5% in the driest third of years, 27.3% in the middle third and 35% in the wettest: the engine's water logic matches 25 years of real farmer behavior. The classification is not yet validated against the INTA national crop map.
- Climate twin: for a warming scenario of +1 to +3 C, we search the whole planet for the place whose current monthly temperature and rainfall (NASA POWER climatology) and soil (SoilGrids: clay, sand, organic carbon, pH, available water) best match the field. With +2 C, the demo field near Casilda behaves like the San Justo area, about 220 km north (1 C is about 140 km). MODIS shows less double cropping there (16.9% vs 25.9%) and later summer crops. The +2 C value is a scenario, not a forecast. Climate analogues exist since 2011 (CGIAR CCAFS); our addition is reading 25 years of satellite records at the twin.

WHAT WE TESTED AND DROPPED
Using GRACE water mass or analogue seasons to forecast the coming season did not beat simpler baselines (r = 0.18 for analogue seasons), so Rastrojo measures risk with real seasons and does not forecast.

TOOLS
Python 3.12, Pydantic v2, FastAPI, Vite, React 19, Leaflet, Vercel; rasterio, numpy and xarray for the satellite prototypes. Tests: Python, Vitest and end-to-end.

IMPACT AND NEXT STEPS
Owner, tenant, cooperative and bank can look at the same field with the same evidence, and a lease can ask for a soil-friendly rotation and check it from space. Next: validate every assumption with AFA, bring NISAR soil moisture and 30 m HLS imagery down to field scale, and use NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections instead of a free warming slider.

TEAM
A team from Rosario, Argentina: Lucas Pippo, Agustin Delmonti, Wenceslao Hernandez and Luciano Raffagnini. Software, electronics and economics. Rastrojo was written during the hackathon.

SOURCE CODE (MIT license): https://github.com/agustindelmonti/nasa-space-apps-2026
